item.title: The Night of the Hunter, 1955 - ★★★★★
item.description:
STILL ASTOUNDING! 

Paddle down the river past all creatures and you will emerge into a new realm where the protector and the perpetrator harmonize with one another. Lean on Jesus indeed!!! 

So much depth and meaning all across this movie. I see new things every time. 

When the kids arrive on the shores of Rachel’s house. John says “don’t hurt her!” And Rachel says, “hurt
Her nothin!’ Wash hers more like it!” Very intentional line with all the religious imagery. These kids are being baptized into a new reality. A new world. One where they are given a wash. A bed. Dignity. Unconditional love and presents on Christmas morning.

item.title: Mr. Smith Goes to Washington, 1939 - ★★★★★
item.description:
Triumphant!!! Guess I’m a sucker for Capra. Makes me want to visit Washington. I truly was on the edge of my seat for this one. How do your write a script with such zip and delight that carries for a whole feature?! Great set pieces and tension and fantastic characters.

Stewart was great as always. Harry Carey as the President was delightful. Jean Arthur ruled. And Eugene Pallette as that guy with the crazy eyebrows who is constantly running to the phone in a panic was such an important reason why I loved this movie so much. 

This movie is just filled out. There isn’t a wasted second. There isn’t a dull moment. There isn’t a dull frame or a dull character. Magnificent! 

(Again a movie I’m sure I saw as a kid at my grandparents. But I forget everything. They loved James Stewart).

item.title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie, 1976 - ★★★★½
item.letterboxd:filmTitle: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
item.description:
What can I say…. I loved it. 

Amazing performances. Reminds me of early Michael Mann. The way this was shot was so unique and interesting. Loved the use of red. The shots of traffic. The lights inside and outside. All creates such a mood and a sense of anxiety. Cassavetes builds tension so much differently than anyone else. 

(Sean Baker and the Safdies would not exist without John Cassavetes. He helped create an American language in the 70s. And you can see it here. You can see it in Mean Streets and Taxi Driver. You can see it in Good Time and Marty Supreme and Lenny Cooke. You can see it in Mikey and Nicky. You can see it in Take-Out and Prince of Broadway and Anora.) 

Can’t wait to finish the Cassavetes canon.
